title: Resh
hookLine: rosh, head, as in Rosh Hashanah

lines: ROSH HASHANAH IN THE SEVENTH MONTH.
cards: When does the Jewish year begin? Still in Egypt, before the Exodus, God tells Moses and Aaron about a month in spring.

In the King James words: "This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you." Yet the Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, falls in autumn, in the seventh month.
In the Torah, that day is simply the first day of the seventh month, a day of blowing the horn. So, spring or fall? The answer turns on one small word.

teach.h: ROSH: HEAD, AS IN ROSH HASHANAH.
teach.b: Resh makes an r sound, and it begins rosh, head. Rosh Hashanah is literally the head of the year. Four parts.
First, the heads of the year.

The Mishnah, in the tractate named for this holiday, answers our puzzle: there are four new years. One in spring, for counting the reign of kings and the order of the festivals. One in late summer, for tithing animals.
One in autumn, for counting years. One in winter, for trees. A year can have more than one head, depending on what you're counting.

From rosh comes reshit, beginning. The Torah's first word, bereshit, in the beginning, carries it. So does a line in Psalms, in the King James words: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom."
Resh looks a lot like dalet, the door; the difference is one corner, sharp on dalet, rounded on resh. In the Shema, the last letter of echad, one, is a dalet, and scribes write it large.
Some commentators say it's so no one mistakes it for a resh, which would turn one into acher, another.

Fourth, the head itself. Rosh is the part of you that goes first, that sees before the hands move. Rosh Hashanah isn't only a new number on the calendar; it's a day for taking stock before the year runs.
A head, in this tradition, is a place to start from, and a place to think from.

how: Jews celebrate Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year, on the first day of the seventh month, with the blowing of the shofar; the Mishnah in tractate Rosh Hashanah counts four new years for different purposes.

o: the letter that begins rosh, the word for head
a letter whose name means the start of spring
the last letter, which ends the word for truth

p: the first day of the seventh month

s: the Mishnah says the Jewish year has only one new year
it counts four, for kings and festivals, animal tithes, years, and trees.
in the Torah, Rosh Hashanah is called by its date
the first day of the seventh month, a day of blowing the horn.
resh and dalet differ by one corner
dalet's corner is sharp; resh's is rounded.

games.q: you're asked when the Jewish year begins: spring, which Exodus calls the beginning of months, or autumn, when Rosh Hashanah falls. what does the Mishnah say?
o: there are four new years, for different things.
games.why: the Mishnah opens tractate Rosh Hashanah with four new years. a year can have more than one head.

practice: Bring to mind something you'll do later on autopilot: replying to a message, walking into a meeting, picking up your phone the moment you're bored.

Give it a head with three quiet questions, what am I about to do, why, and what would I like to come of it, and picture yourself pausing for one breath before you begin. If you pray, you can ask for a clear head.

wordCard.voice: Resh. The letter of rosh, head, and of reshit, beginning: the head of the year, the head of wisdom. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: head; also beginning or chief. The rosh of Rosh Hashanah.

carryVoice: Your line: resh for rosh. A year, and a day, can start from the head. See you tomorrow.
